title: Communicating with patients
blurb: Verbal and non-verbal communication, barriers and how to overcome them, interpreters, active listening and checking understanding.
question: An older patient who is hard of hearing has come for an extraction with her son, who keeps speaking for her. She nods at everything but looks worried. Your mask is on and the suction is running. How can the team make sure she really understands and agrees?

teach.body: GDC Principle 2 says you must communicate effectively with patients. Communication isn't just what you say: it is whether the patient receives and understands the message, and whether you understand them. Good communication underpins valid consent, safe treatment, calmer patients and fewer complaints. As the nurse you're often the person patients feel able to talk to, so you are well placed to notice when something hasn't landed.

children.label: Non-verbal
children.sub: Face, eye contact, posture, gesture, touch

teach.caption: Most conversations use all three at once. If your words and your body language disagree, patients tend to believe the body language.
A barrier at any stage (jargon, noise, hearing loss, language, anxiety) breaks the cycle. Feedback tells you whether the message arrived intact.

teach.body: Watch the patient: white knuckles, a fixed stare, no eye contact or silence can signal anxiety, pain or a communication difficulty. A nod doesn't prove understanding: patients with limited English, hearing loss or nerves often nod to be polite. Your own signals matter too. Masks hide your expression, so use a calm tone, your eyes and gestures. For important conversations, sit the patient upright, face them at eye level, lower your mask when it's safe to do so, and switch off the suction.

head: Barrier
What helps
rows: Face them, lower the mask, cut noise, use a hearing loop or write it down
Professional interpreter, not family or children
Large print, describe what you are doing before you do it
Easy read, short steps, involve their carer
Calm tone, agree a stop signal, allow time
teach.caption: In England, the Accessible Information Standard requires NHS-funded services to identify, record, flag, share and meet patients' communication needs.

steps.label: Give full attention
steps.sub: Don't interrupt or look at the screen

teach.body: Use plain language, short sentences and one point at a time. Then check, using 'teach-back': 'Just so I know I've explained it clearly, can you tell me what you'll do if it bleeds tonight?' Invite questions, and ask the dentist to pause if the patient wants to ask something. Open questions ('How are you feeling about today?') get more information than closed ones ('Are you OK?'). If you don't know an answer, say you'll find out and come back. Questions about the quality of treatment go to the dentist.

Use a professional interpreter, face-to-face, by phone or video, or a BSL interpreter for Deaf patients. Avoid relying on family, and never on children: they may not translate accurately, the patient may hold back, and confidentiality is lost. Book extra time, speak to the patient rather than the interpreter, and record that an interpreter was used. When collecting any patient from the waiting room, introduce yourself and your role, confirm their identity, and explain what will happen.

teach.text: A nod is not understanding. Patients nod to be polite, because they're anxious, or because they didn't hear. Always check with teach-back, especially when consent depends on it.

items: Communication is verbal, non-verbal, and written or visual; it only works if the message is understood.
Identify barriers (hearing, language, sight, learning disability, anxiety, jargon) and adapt.
Use professional interpreters, not family or children; record that one was used.
Active listening: stop, face, attend, acknowledge, reflect.
Plain words, open questions, teach-back; if you don't know, find out and come back.

summary: You can now describe the types of communication and the communication cycle, spot and overcome common barriers, work with interpreters, listen actively, and check a patient's understanding using plain language and teach-back.

A.q: After the dentist explains post-extraction care, what is the best way to check the patient has understood?
options: Give them a leaflet to read later
Ask them to explain it back to you
Repeat it all again, more slowly and loudly
A.why: Teach-back, asking the patient to explain in their own words, shows whether they've genuinely understood.

whyNot.0: A closed question invites a polite 'yes' that may not reflect understanding.
whyNot.1: A leaflet helps, but doesn't check understanding now.
whyNot.3: Volume doesn't fix a misunderstanding and can feel patronising.

A.q: A patient with limited English nods throughout the explanation of her treatment. What should you conclude?
options: She would rather not talk now
A.why: Nodding can be politeness or nerves. With a language barrier, understanding must be checked, ideally with an interpreter.

whyNot.2: Agreement needs to be informed, which can't be assumed.
whyNot.3: Nodding doesn't tell you she doesn't want to talk.

A.q: Which is an example of non-verbal communication?
options: Tone of voice on the phone
A.why: Body language, such as gripping the chair, is non-verbal and may signal anxiety.

whyNot.0: Tone is part of how spoken words are delivered.
whyNot.1: An appointment card is written communication.
whyNot.2: A text message is written communication.

B.q: A Deaf patient who lip-reads is in the chair. What will help most?
options: Speak louder from behind the chair
Face the patient and lower your mask
Keep the suction running to save time
B.why: Lip-readers need to see your face clearly, so face them, lower your mask when safe and reduce background noise.

whyNot.0: Volume doesn't help someone who lip-reads, and they can't see you from behind.
whyNot.2: The patient has a right to be spoken to directly.
whyNot.3: Background noise makes communication harder for everyone.

B.q: A patient attends with little English. Who is the most appropriate person to interpret?
options: A receptionist who knows a little
Another patient in the waiting room
B.why: Professional interpreters are trained, accurate and bound by confidentiality.

whyNot.0: Children must not be used: it's inappropriate and they may not translate accurately.
whyNot.1: Partial language skills risk errors in important information.
whyNot.2: This breaches confidentiality and is unreliable.

B.q: A patient asks you a question about their treatment that you can't answer. What should you do?
options: Say you'll find out and come back
Suggest they look it up on the NHS website
B.why: Be honest, find the correct answer (usually from the dentist) and get back to the patient.

whyNot.2: General information online may not apply to their treatment; they need an answer about their own care.

C.q: Which of these is part of active listening?
options: Planning your reply as they speak
C.why: Reflecting back ('So your main worry is…') shows you've listened and lets the patient correct you.

whyNot.0: Looking at a screen signals you aren't fully listening.
whyNot.1: Planning a reply means you're not fully attending to what they say.
whyNot.3: Interrupting stops the patient explaining in their own words.

C.q: Which question is most likely to encourage an anxious patient to share their worries?
options: 'You're not feeling nervous at all, are you?'
C.why: An open question invites the patient to explain in their own words.

whyNot.1: A closed question usually gets a one-word answer.
whyNot.2: A leading question pushes them to say they're fine.
whyNot.3: This moves on without inviting their concerns.

C.q: Collecting a new patient from the waiting room, what should you do first?
options: Ask about their medical history aloud
Walk ahead and let them follow
C.why: Introducing yourself and your role, then confirming identity, puts the patient at ease and is safe practice.

whyNot.0: Medical details shouldn't be discussed in a public area.
whyNot.1: This feels unwelcoming and you haven't confirmed who they are.
whyNot.2: Treatment explanations come in the surgery, after confirming identity.

reteach.title: Like a radio signal
reteach.question: Think of a message as a radio broadcast. What can cause static, and how do you know the listener got the message?

blocks.body: You are the transmitter and the patient is the receiver. Static is anything that scrambles the signal: suction noise, a mask hiding your mouth, jargon, a language the patient doesn't share, hearing loss, or fear so strong they can't take anything in. Turning up the volume rarely helps. Clear the static instead: quiet room, face to face, plain words, an interpreter, and time. Then ask the receiver to repeat the message back. That's teach-back.

blocks.text: Talking to the companion instead of the patient is disrespectful and can mean the patient's own views are never heard. Speak to the patient first, and involve the companion only as they wish.

explain.body: Verbal (words, tone), non-verbal (face, posture, gestures, eye contact) and written or visual (leaflets, models). Non-verbal signals can show anxiety or pain before words do.

test.q: A patient answers questions but avoids eye contact and is very quiet. What might this indicate?
options: They want the treatment to go much faster
test.why: Non-response or little eye contact can signal anxiety, pain or a communication difficulty, so check gently.

whyNot.0: Jumping to 'rude' ignores likely causes such as nerves.
whyNot.3: There is nothing to suggest this.

explain.body: Hearing or sight loss, limited English, learning disability, anxiety, noise and jargon. Adapt: face them, cut noise, plain words, easy read, professional interpreters.

test.q: Which is the best way to explain 'gingivitis' to a patient?
options: Use the term and move on
Write the word down for them
Spell it out letter by letter
test.why: Plain language helps the patient understand. Jargon is a barrier.

whyNot.0: The patient may not know the term.
whyNot.2: Writing a technical term doesn't explain it.
whyNot.3: Spelling it doesn't explain what it means.

explain.body: Short sentences, one point at a time, invite questions, then teach-back. If you don't know an answer, find out and come back.

options: Giving the patient a written leaflet to keep
The patient explains it back to you
test.why: Teach-back asks the patient to explain, in their own words, what they've been told, to confirm understanding.

whyNot.1: Teach-back is about the patient's understanding.
whyNot.2: A leaflet supports understanding but doesn't check it.
